title: The Friction is Your Judgment — Armin Ronacher & Cristina Poncela Cubeiro, Earendil
talk_summary: Armin Ronacher and Cristina Poncela Cubeiro argue that agent-generated code optimizes for 'making progress' and produces more failure conditions and entropy than human code, so teams must deliberately reintroduce friction where human judgment matters. They propose agent-legible codebases (modularization, lint-enforced mechanical rules, no hidden magic) and review tooling that separates mechanical fixes from human-judgment callouts like migrations and permission changes.

takeaways.technique: Split review output into auto-fixable mechanical issues vs. human-judgment callouts
takeaways.what_they_do: Their PR review extension separates mechanical bugs (lint/H1D violations) that the agent can auto-fix from a distinct 'human callout' section for changes like DB migrations and permissioning that require a person's judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we specifically call out the kind of changes where the human's brain should reactivate

takeaways.technique: Lint-enforced mechanical rules to catch agent failure modes
takeaways.what_they_do: They encode agent-typical defects as lint rules (no bare catch, single SQL query interface, one UI primitives library, no dynamic imports, unique function names) so violations are caught mechanically rather than by review.

takeaways.technique: Agent-legible codebase: modularize code flow and remove hidden magic
takeaways.what_they_do: They structure code so agents can add a feature in one spot, define clear step boundaries in code flow, avoid ORM/React-server-action indirection that hides intent, and enforce unique function names for grep/token efficiency.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if the agent can't see something, it can surely not respect it

takeaways.technique: Keep humans on architecture/reliability, delegate reproduction and exploration
takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly partition work: agents excel at reproducing customer issues and exploring product directions, but system architecture and reliability require going slow with human judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: system architecture, creating reliability in the system, they are not just very good at

takeaways.technique: Recognize review-capacity amplification and cap PR size
takeaways.what_they_do: They note agents produce far more code than review capacity, causing rubber-stamped reviews, and argue for small PRs and treating large diffs as a signal to slow down.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every engineer has a multitude of producing power compared to their reviewing power

takeaways.what_they_do: They call out agent code that loads defaults when a config file is missing, which hides misconfiguration until bad data is written; humans feel bad writing this, agents don't.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it doesn't read a config file, it loads some defaults ... I might only discover that I have a massive problem after 2 hours
